html:
The Caloosahatchee culture is an archaeological culture of the Gulf coast of southwest Florida, lasting from about 500 BCE to 1750. Its land ran from southern Sarasota County through Charlotte and Lee counties to the northern edge of Collier County, and about 90 kilometres inland. At the time of first European contact it was the core of the Calusa domain.

The coast here is a rich estuary: bays and sounds behind barrier islands, full of fish and shellfish. People were already working the waters of Charlotte Harbor intensively before 3500 BCE. Plain pottery of the early Glades culture appeared around 500 BCE, and a local style grew out of it around 500 CE.

What makes this culture stand out is that it built a complex society without farming. By about 800 CE the population was dense, and fish and shellfish fed chiefs, priests and large towns. People built shell mounds, canals and causeways. Mound Key in Estero Bay was the Calusa capital when the Spanish arrived.

Archaeologists divide its history into five periods by pottery. The later periods are marked by pottery from other traditions arriving through trade.

The Calusa met Juan Ponce de León in 1513 and fought off Spanish attempts to settle. A Spanish fort and mission at Mound Key in the 1560s soon failed. Disease, and slave raids by peoples allied to English Carolina in the early 1700s, broke the society. By the mid 1700s the last Calusa had left for Cuba or joined other peoples. The Timucua to the north suffered a similar fate.
